Trump faces new political reality as Democrats vow investigations
items.description: President Donald Trump was left to grapple on Thursday with the stinging rebuke from voters after a midterm election rout, while triumphant Democrats vowed to lower prices and combat the “cartel” within the White House in the new Congress. Trump faces a radically transformed and hostile political landscape after Democrats seized both the House of Representatives and the Senate in Tuesday’s midterms. The result was a personal humiliation for the 80-year-old Trump, leaving him as a lame duck president for the remaining two years of his term and signaling an end to his stranglehold on the Republican Party. Vice President JD Vance publicly split with Trump over the Iran war a day after the vote, saying the conflict was the “reason we lost” as he distanced himself from the unpopular war ahead of a possible 2028 White House run . “The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote in a long social media post. “The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next six years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a ​worthwhile cost to pay.” Democrats by early Thursday morning had control of 54 Senate seats and a strong majority in the House. Two Senate races — in heavily Republican Mississippi and Alaska — remained too close to call. Shift shows only states with a 2026 Senate race and in which 95pc or more of expected votes have been counted. —Reuters Democrats have vowed investigations into Trump and his administration and said the incoming majority would be focused on accountability and affordability. “The massive corruption the country has experienced from the Trump Cartel explains why very little is getting done to help everyday Americans,” House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Wednesday in a letter announcing his candidacy for speaker of the House. “That changes immediately,” he said, adding Democrats are “going to hold the crooks accountable”. It will be the first time that Trump, a Republican who also held the White House from 2017 to 2021, has had to contend with a Democratic-controlled Congress in both chambers. Jeffries said the incoming majority will be focused on affordability and accountability. “We don’t work for Donald Trump,” the New York lawmaker told reporters on Wednesday. “We work for the American people. And the days of the House of Representatives functioning like ​a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump administration are over.” New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has emerged as a national Democratic figure since his election a year ago, released a video on social media urging his party to address the concerns ​of voters burdened by rising prices who want schools and roads. “It is not enough to simply win power. We must use it,” Mamdani said. “Now, it’s time for us in the Democratic Party to deliver.” Once seated in January, Democrats are expected to use their power to investigate Trump’s administration, family and allies and demand concessions on major legislation. The Democratic Senate can block Trump’s nominees, including any US Supreme Court justices should a vacancy arise. The Democratic victory is fuelling questions about the longevity of the Supreme Court’s two eldest justices, Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito, and the durability of its conservative majority. In the meantime, Republicans hold the reins and will have at least one must-pass piece of legislation ahead — a measure to fund the federal government past December — that they could use to enact conservative priorities during the so-called lame-duck period. The loss also upended Republicans’ House leadership, with House Speaker Mike Johnson saying he would not continue to lead his caucus next year. Trump had no public events scheduled for Thursday, according to a White House press schedule. First Lady Melania Trump was set to host officials from Moscow and Kyiv at the White House ahead of talks in Abu Dhabi aimed at ending the Ukraine war . ‘Worst-case scenario’ Trump has attempted to brush off the election results. He spent the beginning of his first public appearance on Wednesday talking to reporters about the marble and Corinthian columns of his new $400 million ballroom . US President Donald Trump looks at the final steel beam as it is lifted on the day it goes into the ballroom, at the White House in Washington, DC, US, November 4, 2026. —Reuters But he conceded that what Vance had said about the Iran war was “largely true because it drove the gasoline up” — a key issue for voters angered by the rising cost of living. “But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again. Because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear weapon,” he said. Trump added that he would “get along” with Democrats, repeating the conciliatory tone he took as the results emerged on Tuesday night, but repeated his threat to veto legislation that he didn’t like. He warned that if his foes tried to impeach him for a third time it would “destroy” the Democratic Party. Still, he remains the head of a party now wrestling with a resounding defeat that could spark Republican infighting. Democratic wave Democrats focused their campaign on corruption and affordability, blaming Trump’s expensive tariffs on imports, some of which were ruled to be an illegal tax by the courts, and the ​war with Iran for driving up ⁠costs while highlighting the billions of dollars the Trump family has made since he returned to the White House. Republicans, led by Trump, attacked Democrats for defending transgender people’s rights and similar social issues, portraying them as radical and extreme. Voters made it clear they were more concerned with pocketbook issues. Trump had cast the midterm elections as a referendum on the first half of his second four-year stint in the White House, repeatedly urging his Republican base to “pretend I’m on the ballot”, a message that Democratic Party leaders were happy to amplify. The result: voters in conservative strongholds who had propelled the president to his second term in office just two years ago swung dramatically toward Democrats, fueled by deep frustration over the unpopular war with Iran, anxiety over the high ​cost of living and anger at Trump’s stewardship of the country. In Texas, the biggest Republican-led state before Tuesday, Democrats ended a decades-long losing streak in seismic fashion, winning their first Senate seat there since 1988 and ousting three-term Governor Greg Abbott. Kansas elected its first Democratic senator ​since the Great Depression nearly a century ago, and in South Carolina, a state that Trump carried by nearly 18 points in 2024, Democrats turned aside his hand-picked Senate candidate. “This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last 100 years,” Florida Republican Governor Ron DeSantis said in public remarks on the results. DeSantis, who ran for president against Trump in 2024, noted Florida, where Trump-backed Byron Donalds became the state’s first Black governor and Ashley Moody retained a Senate seat, was the only bright spot for Republicans this week. “This is going to last far beyond just two years,” he said of Republicans’ election defeat. “We just have to be very clear-eyed. This is probably the political worst-case scenario for a midterm election.”

items.title: Even Where MAGA Won, MAGA Lost
items.description: One of the biggest Republican wins in an otherwise-terrible midterm night for the GOP was the victory of the Trump-supporting Byron Donalds in Florida’s race for governor. Donalds will become the first Black governor of that state. If you could resurrect Jefferson Davis and tell him that the governor of Florida will be a Black Republican married to a white woman, he would crawl straight back into his coffin. That this was MAGA’s big win in a night of defeats is remarkable, given the movement’s hostility toward diversity , and its nostalgia for an America where rigid race and gender hierarchies were enforced by the state. Even where Republicans won, in other words, President Trump’s racially exclusive conception of American citizenship lost. Trump could browbeat corporate America into eliminating DEI programs; he could threaten colleges to let in fewer students of color; he could direct the full power of the federal government toward deporting immigrants. But he could not will away the America that actually exists. The America that emerges from the midterm elections is not the monochrome world of Madison Avenue ad campaigns from the 1950s. It is a diverse country, made up of many different kinds of people, all of whom are American. The victories of Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Aaron Ford in Nevada, and David Crowley in Wisconsin, in addition to that of Donalds, mean that there will be more Black governors than ever in U.S. history. In Texas, where Mexican Americans were subject to legalized forms of racial discrimination until the mid-20th century, Gina Hinojosa will become the first Hispanic governor. Xavier Becerra is the first Hispanic governor to be elected in California, and Deb Haaland will become New Mexico’s first Native American governor. Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota will become the first Native American woman elected to the U.S. Senate. And Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan will become the first Muslim U.S. senator. [ Read: Repudiation ] This happened despite the president, and the many Republicans who followed his lead, trying to make the midterms about a familiar theme: the country being invaded by strange people who do not belong here, let alone in the halls of power. President Trump and others called El-Sayed a “ jihadist ,” and Vice President Vance said he should “show a little gratitude to the country that gave him everything.” (Like Vance, El-Sayed was born here.) After El-Sayed won, he told Trump , “I know you struggled with my name. You can just go on and call me Senator.” Republicans fearmongered about “Sharia law” before losing every major statewide office in the Lone Star State. In Minnesota, candidates attacked Somalis, running spots about “Somali gangs” taking over. During a speech in Ohio, Trump went after the Minnesota Democrat Ilhan Omar: “She comes in from a country without laws, without police, without military, without—all they do is shoot each other.” He continued, “They come into the United States of America, and they tell us how to run our country. We’re not going to stand for it.” Trump won in 2016 and in 2024 while leaning into this strategy of scapegoating ethnic and religious minorities, which convinced many politicians and media figures that the strategy was deviously effective, or at least that it didn’t turn too many people off. After all, in 2020 and 2024, Trump grew his coalition, gaining support among Black and Hispanic voters as well as white ones. But the strategy could not overcome the economic headwinds Trump himself created with tariffs and the arguably illegal, inarguably ill-advised war in Iran. Many voters in 2024 also believed that Trump would focus immigration enforcement on criminals, instead of on a violent and indiscriminate campaign that would involve schoolchildren and their families hiding in their homes and masked gunmen shooting Americans dead in the streets. I am not going to make the same mistake as the Trump Republicans after 2024 did and declare a permanent realignment of the U.S. electorate toward my policy preferences. Economic mismanagement and the war were clearly the primary drivers of Democratic success. What these wins do say, however, is that the real America is not the “Real America” of conservative fan fiction inspired by the years 1945 to 1964. Real Americans are not just those whose ancestors came over on the Mayflower, or whose ancestors served in the Revolution or Civil War, or who describe themselves with pathetic euphemisms such as “ Heritage American .” As Abraham Lincoln once said , newcomers who believe in the principle that “all men are created equal” have “a right to claim it as though they were blood of the blood, and flesh of the flesh, of the men who wrote that Declaration; and so they are.” As soon as the returns made the extent of the bloodbath clear, MAGA personalities began blaming the nation’s diversity for Republicans’ losses. The conservative podcaster Benny Johnson posted , “In 1970, the White population in Texas was 89%. In 2000, it was 50%. Now it’s less than 39%. Demographics is destiny.” The Trump adviser Laura Loomer declared , “America was always intended to be a majority White country. Not a cesspool for third world minorities. America was founded as a Christian country. Not a Muslim country.” [ Idrees Kahloon: Why Republicans lost so big ] “Democrats imported millions of foreigners, handed them a bunch of free shit, and then registered them to vote,” the account of the influencer Chaya Raichik posted on X. “If we ever want to win again we need deportations and denaturalizations ramped up on steroids or our country will forever be lost to the communists.” Contrary to Johnson, demographics is not destiny—if it was, Texas would have flipped a long time ago and Trump would not have won there by double digits in 2024. Millions of nonwhite Americans have conservative beliefs, and most of them would be happy to vote for Republicans who treated them as Americans instead of invaders. As for Loomer, not only was America explicitly not founded as a Christian country, but we also fought a civil war over whether it was a white country—and the side taken by Loomer lost . Raichik’s call for ethnic cleansing is grotesque, but it nonetheless illustrates how those on the extreme right see the problem, which is that there are Americans who are not white whose votes count as much as theirs. You cannot call for people to be exiled because of their ethnic background and expect them to vote for you. In September, Trump said , “America does not belong to those who hate it. America belongs to those who love it.” But the way MAGA talks about the America that actually exists—as opposed to the one it imagines once existed—doesn’t sound like love at all. Whether or not Americans believe in multiculturalism, we are multicultural. One is an ideology; the other is a fact.

items.title: Did Democrats Win—Or Did Trump Lose?
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Overcast | Pocket Casts If it wasn’t perfectly obvious going into the midterms, it’s certainly clear now: Democrats, from different states, with different histories and political leanings, all hovered around a unified message, which can be loosely translated to: You can’t afford your life, and someone is responsible for that. Adam Hamilton, the moderate megachurch pastor in Kansas, used a common-sense version: “Lower Costs. Protect Healthcare. Listen to Kansas.” James Talarico of Texas named the perpetrator, calling Elon Musk’s wealth a “spiritual sickness.” Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed connected the perpetrator more closely to the victim, describing MAGA as the ones “picking your pocket.” This discipline resulted from months of research and fine-tuning by the Democratic establishment, according to the Atlantic staff writers Ashley Parker and Michael Scherer. They reported on a coordinated strategy by the Democrats that began with the simple insight that they could not compete with Donald Trump for voters’ attention, so they had to fit their message into the tiny span of attention that people had left. The result, Parker and Scherer explain on Radio Atlantic , was a push from the likely next House speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, to keep the message simple and repetitive. Over time, it evolved into what could be called a soft populism, broad enough to include the midwestern pastor and the Michigan progressive. Like all populist narratives, however, this one has its limits. The party that now controls Congress will shortly discover that Elon Musk is not, in fact, the only reason Americans think that their lives are unaffordable, and that Donald Trump is, in fact, still the president. What will the next two years look like, given that Trump and Jeffries have no relationship? Can either party evolve quickly enough? And can any party meet the voters’ intense expectations? The following is a transcript of the episode: Hanna Rosin: The banner headline from this week is obvious: “Democrats Rout GOP.” “A Historic Blue Wave.” There are still votes left to count, but it is perfectly clear that across the country, across all demographics, in places that haven’t elected Democrats to national office in decades, the voters sent a message. Ashley Parker: The first one that made me go, This is absolutely insane , I think, was South Carolina, which came in pretty early, before Texas even. Michael Scherer: I’ve been watching Election Nights for a long time now. I’m not a big fan of watching prediction markets, ’cause they’re often wrong, but they’re really good close to something happening. And so that was the thing that got me. When I turned into the prediction markets and saw them moving so quickly—and this is, like, hours before, just the first dribbles of votes coming in—it was clear this was not gonna be close at all. [ Music ] Rosin: So yeah, the voters sent a message. But what exactly was the message they were sending? I’m Hanna Rosin. This is Radio Atlantic . The election was clearly a referendum against the status quo, maybe a confirmation that voters bought the Democrats message: Trump is responsible for much of your suffering, and he doesn’t necessarily care . But was it an affirmation of the Democratic platform? No evidence of that yet. And Republicans? They have a leader who acts like a king, controls all the party’s money, but now seems to have none of the voters’ confidence. That’s a hard one. But we’re getting ahead of ourselves. On Wednesday, I talked with staff writers Ashley Parker— Parker: Thanks for having me. Rosin: —and Michael Scherer— Scherer: Thank you. Rosin: —who have inside reporting on how soon-to-be House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries and the Democratic Party pulled this off, and what they’re thinking now. Scherer: The unifying fact of this election is that every Democrat, even from the far left, you know, the democratic-socialist fellow travelers to, you know, the pastor from Kansas, were running on the same message. That was what was remarkable about this cycle. It was, The prices are too high. One of the reasons the prices are too high is that the system is rigged against you, and I’m gonna focus like a laser on that, and I’m gonna fix it for you . And the rest of the stuff just, all the other issues, all the other things that divide Democrats, you know, was brought up by Republicans, but no one cared, because that wasn’t the thing that the American people cared about right now. And, you know, what’s been an emergency for decades now in terms of working-class, middle-class people feeling like they’re falling further and further behind from where they were is now, like, a 10-alarm fire. And you had the sort of salt in the wound of the Iran war and the salt of the wound of gas prices. And so there was just only one issue, and Democrats were all singing from the same playbook. Parker: And this is not quite uniform, because there’s some notable exceptions, and I don’t say this to detract from Democrats’ wins. The wave, or whatever analogy you want, was so big that I think a lot of these people would have won anyhow. But in a lot of cases, they were running against extremely flawed Republican candidates, including extremely flawed Republican candidates who were only candidates because President Trump had pushed them: Darline Graham; there’s Ken Paxton in Texas. You know, Trump pushed Thom Tillis out to retire. You know, an exception, of course, is Susan Collins, who is a perfect senator for that state and lost anyhow. But they were running against some bad candidates and just some kind of generic white guys who were so tied to Trump that they might not have been bad, but they weren’t gonna be able to distance themselves in any authentic way from everything that voters viewed as bad. Rosin: Right. I mean, every state has its own story. We’re talking, you know, about 24 hours after the election. I feel like it’s our job to tell a bigger narrative about the story, and I resist that. But you guys have actually done some reporting that indicates that there is a party story to tell. There was some discipline. So what is it? How did Democrats pull this off? Like, in one sentence, how did they do it? And then we’ll get into the details. Scherer: In one sentence: They inverted the dynamic of the 2024 election, in which Donald Trump won because Democrats weren’t seen as being focused on the main thing. Rosin: Okay, two sentences. Scherer: Sorry. Rosin: Say more, so— Scherer: There was a comma. It was a compound sentence. Rosin: Okay. So let’s start the story at the beginning. There’s such an interesting revelation that you both wrote about, which has to do with voter attention span. It seems like that’s kind of the starting point of their discipline. Can you explain that? Like, what they discovered about how people are paying attention. Scherer: In the spring of 2025, a media consultant comes to talk to House Democratic leadership and says, Look, you guys have to understand what you’re dealing with. The average American voter spends about four minutes a week thinking about politics, and three and a half minutes a week is focused on whatever Donald Trump’s doing. So you got 30 seconds you’re competing with everything else about . And as you work out 30 seconds by waking hours—I did the quick division. It’s 0.007 percent of waking hours that Democrats have as an opportunity to even engage. And so— Rosin: It’s, like, one scroll on your phone. Scherer: Right. Rosin: It’s so concrete and so insane, but interesting. Scherer: 30 seconds a week. And so, you know, Hakeem Jeffries and other Democrats thought, Look, we’re never going to be able to win more of those four minutes. That’s not the goal. All we have to do is make something of the 30 seconds we have . And so Hakeem adopted, basically, as a sort of motto, which he repeated endlessly, Simplicity and repetition . And they just started hammering. From his first speech, you know, before Trump’s inauguration in 2025, this idea that the dynamics that had wrecked Democrats in 2024 were going to still be dominant in 2026: the economy, inflation, costs, affordability—I mean, affordability wasn’t even really a word at that point, but it sort of became the way of framing it—and that they would be the party that focused like a laser on that, and said every time they stood up, That’s the thing we’re concerned about . And what was interesting is then, as the year goes on, lots of other things happen. Immigration comes up. There’s, you know, immigration raids. There’s Jeffrey Epstein. There’s corruption, all this other stuff. They keep returning, whatever the issue was of the day, back to this, How is it impacting you? Corruption was not about Donald Trump getting rich. It was about the fact that Donald Trump’s getting rich or his family’s getting rich has a direct effect on whether you have money in your pocket. And then they were just given this gift from the president, who could not for the life of him focus at all on that issue. I mean, he was allergic to it. He said affordability was a hoax. Rosin: So you start out with this creative constraint. You got 30 seconds to give your message: It’s affordability. But then it seems to evolve. Like, it’s affordability plus an enemy, like a reason you can’t afford it. Like, how does the message become a little more complicated over time and take different forms in different candidates? Parker: Well, again, I mean, it is affordability, and I think initially from some of the Democrats we talked to, there was skepticism when these issues of corruption came up. And not just of corruption, but also of some of the tech oligarchs that Donald Trump was surrounding himself with, with some of the wealth of his Cabinet. And, you know, I talked to one Democratic pollster who told me, you know, I could not imagine that this would be an effective closing message with Democrats , or with voters, because it wasn’t just Democrats who showed up and voted for Democrats. But as Michael said, what they quickly realized—and part of this was a focus-group project that the Democratic Senate group did—was that corruption was so closely linked with cost of living for voters, and the sense that Donald Trump and Republicans did not care about voters like that. And so to go back to 2024, the most devastating ad that the Trump campaign ran was against Kamala Harris, and it talked about: They had her on camera supporting using federal funds for sex changes for transgender prisoners. And they said—the tagline was, Kamala Harris— Rosin: Kamala Harris is for they/them. President Trump is for you. No one will ever forget that ad. Parker: Yes. Campaign ad: Kamala supports taxpayer-funded sex changes for prisoners and illegal aliens. Kamala Harris: Every transgender inmate would have access. Campaign ad: Kamala’s for they/them. President Trump is for you. Parker: And when, in the moment talking to Democrats, they said, Look, voters are not actually going to the polls and voting on whether or not we’re using federal dollars for gender-reassignment surgery for transgender inmates. That’s not, like, a top-20 voting issue, but the reason it is so devastatingly effective is because it shows that in a moment when voters are hurting, she is not focused on you. Her attention is elsewhere . And that is the exact same thing that in this case corruption did for Democrats against Trump, and it was fascinating because they tried to rerun that “they/them” ad again in some of these races, against James Talarico in Texas surgeries on children. Campaign ad: And even said parents were abusive if they opposed turning their boy into a girl. James Talarico stands with them, not with us. Parker: And it doesn’t work. When it is a pocketbook issue and you feel that the president, and the party in charge, doesn’t care about the fact that at the end of the month, you’re maybe waiting to go to the grocery store until your next paycheck comes in, they could care less who’s swimming in what meet. Scherer: There’s a remarkable interview that Gina Hinojosa, who’s the governor-elect of Texas, gave in the middle of the campaign—I think it was a podcast, I think with The New York Times —in which she’s asked why she no longer refers to herself as a progressive or a liberal. And she was very clear in that campaign: I’m not a progressive or a liberal . She talked about herself as a populist. And she is a liberal. I mean, she’s a progressive liberal who just won the governorship of Texas. But her answer was, Liberal means social issues, and I don’t care about social issues right now. That is not what matters. What matters is populous issues, which means people in power are preventing us from getting what we need, and that is the issue of the day . Gina Hinojosa: I just think that progressive politics is associated with culture wars, and I have no interest in fighting culture wars at this time. Fighting culture wars at this time is not a winnable fight. It is the fight that divides us because it is the fight about who we are in our lived experiences. Scherer: And so it was a complete redefinition of what it means to be a Democrat, what it means to be really a liberal. To be a liberal now is to, in this campaign at least, whether you were [Abdul] El-Sayed in Michigan or a pastor from Kansas, what it means is to be saying, You are getting shortchanged by people in power, and I’m going to focus on that and fix it when I get there . Rosin: Right. It’s like tying together affordability— you can’t afford anything —with corruption. Like, that was the move. ’Cause I’m thinking of the different ways that it came out. There’s Jon Ossoff’s version: Most corrupt administration in American history . There’s El-Sayed’s version: Every time they say my name and faith, they have their hand in your pocket . It’s like people just tailored this particular connective message to their platform, whatever their platform was. Parker: And there’s also the ballroom, which is both corruption in how it’s getting paid and how it was done, but is also sort of a physical, tangible reminder, in part because Donald Trump legitimately is obsessed with it and can’t stop talking about it. Again, he’s not focused on you. When he comes out to talk about the Iran war and how he’s trying to end it and instead lifts up three, you know, dioramas of the ballroom, that doesn’t reassure voters. And that also, stunningly, was essentially his closing argument on Monday, standing in front of the Reflecting Pool and talking about beautification projects in Washington, D.C. Rosin: You know what’s even more remarkable? Today, Wednesday, the day we’re recording this, Trump gave a press conference. I don’t know if you guys tuned into it. Parker: We did. Rosin: He’s talking about specifics of the marble in the ballroom. President Trump: We ordered the marble for the floor. The marble is really magnificent marble. It’s a cut—it’s a vein that people have been after for 50 years. Rosin: It is as if he was asleep all day yesterday. Scherer: He signed the steel beam. Rosin: Yeah. “Love.” Scherer: Yeah, “Love.” ( Laughs .) That’s right. Rosin: What is that about? Scherer: I mean, we wrote a story several months ago now, “ The YOLO Presidency ,” and that was really about, I think, like, the defining characteristic of Trump’s second term, which is that he is doing everything he’s always wanted to do, and he has always seen the world through his own prism, and he is still seeing it through his own prism. I think, like, the tension right now in Washington is how much the sort of narcissism and selfishness of the president is going to face a rebellion in his party or not. So far, they’ve been very quiet, but now they have a lot of reason to actually rebel, and that’s gonna be very interesting to watch. But he’s not showing, you know, much introspection there. I think he still believes that one of his greatest legacies will be beautifying Washington, D.C., regardless of what voters say in polls. Rosin: I mean, the thing about narcissism is: It’s both extremely big and extremely small. And the two of you have written about both aspects of it—the grandiosity, like, I run the country; I run the world , that I think was also the headline of one of your stories. Parker: Yes. Rosin: And also the ability to just narrow the focus to such, like, a tiny pinpoint and absolutely ignore the audience and everything around you. Parker: Well, it’s also just great to be Donald Trump right now, to hear him tell it, right? It’s that he has nothing to do with this loss. Had he been on the ballot, Republicans would’ve won, and those who lost were horrible candidates, and he had no choice but to try to lift them across the finish line, but there’s only so much you can do for these mediocre candidates . And you know what? At a certain level, he believes it. [ Music ] Rosin: After the break: what the next two years of divided government might look like, and what to expect going into 2028. [ Break ] Rosin: Okay, the election is over—almost over. It’s not quite over. There’s still votes to be counted, but let’s still look at what’s coming. First, I wanna get your thoughts on something that Vice President J. D. Vance tweeted on Wednesday. It’s part of a longer tweet. It’s about the war. It reads. in part, quote: The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night. If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost [to pay]. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest. But [everyone] knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there. So this is the beginning of recriminations. Why did we lose? What do we do now? What do you read into this? Parker: Well, first I just wanna take a step back and say it was already weird enough to have a vice president who was sort of a Twitter troll, right? Arguing with people whose photo was an egg, and now he’s leapt into the punditry game. I mean, it is just wild to have a sitting vice president who is messaging to the nation and behaving in this way. So that’s the broader macro, and then Michael, you can take the specifics of Iran. Scherer: Well, no, and the other thing is: I don’t know if Americans tuned in, but Vance has been on the road for a month and a half. He’s been doing TV, town halls, and big speeches, and in almost every one of them, he defends the Iran war. He’s on the record. He basically was on the campaign trail saying, This was something we needed to do. We don’t want Iran to have a nuclear weapon . He has also tried to maintain that he was a skeptic always early on. We’ve had leaks from the White House about the degree to which he was skeptical of the president’s decision and pushing back on the president’s decision. But this is about him trying to salvage the Republican Party for 2028. Rosin: Okay. So this is him beginning the process of repositioning possibly himself or possibly the party, and actually I wanna get into that. But first, the next two years: Congress and the president are gonna have to work together. You guys were reporting on Hakeem Jeffries. What do you know about his relationship with the president? Scherer: There is basically no relationship. They’ve been in the same room during the inauguration, and then there was one meeting at the White House before the shutdown in the fall of 2025, in which, as it was recounted to me, he walks in with Chuck Schumer, the president says, Hey, do you guys want some Diet Cokes? They both say no, and someone puts Diet Cokes in front of them, and then as they’re talking, someone puts Trump 2028 hats in front of them, and then a photographer starts circling them, trying to get photos of Hakeem and Schumer with the Trump 2028 hats. I mean, it was like a circus of a meeting. Now, that said, Hakeem is, I think, very serious about what he’s been saying, which is that he believes the future of the Democratic Party is actually finding a way to deliver on this simple and repetitive message they’ve had, which means, I don’t think—I mean, it is gonna be an ugly relationship. There was a point last year where Hakeem Jeffries stood in front of a camera and said, “F Donald Trump.” Like, they are not on great terms. But they are gonna try and work together, and think there are areas in which they can work together. One of the things the president’s very proud of are things that have lowered costs. The most-favored-nation drug-company deals, the no tax on tips, the no tax on Social Security, the Trump Accounts for kids—those things can all be expanded. There’s gonna be fights over Medicaid funding. There’s gonna be fights over Obamacare subsidies. But one of the interesting things here is, like, how Republicans choose to engage with Democrats and try and reposition themselves now before 2028, because it’s very clear to the Republican Party that if they don’t get back on the right side of this one issue, and another issue doesn’t pop up, I mean, this has been the one issue for 30 years, so it’s probably not gonna be a different issue next time. But if they don’t get back on the right side of this issue, they’re in a lot of trouble. Rosin: In some ways, what you just outlined is the most positive version of a scenario of what could happen. There’s a whole other version— Parker: Do you want me to do the dystopia? Rosin: You can do the negative one, the dystopia, sure. But aside from it being a dystopia, there is a legitimate reading of this election that it’s about accountability, that this was a moment of reckoning and accountability. The nation had reached its limit. They’re tired of corruption. And that implies showdowns. Like, Who are we gonna investigate for this corruption? How are we gonna restore certain government institutions? And that’s likely to be, like, real warfare. So is that the apocalyptic scenario, or is there an even worse one? Parker: So first I should also say, just on the positive scenario, is: For all of the tension that Trump may have in his relationships with Democrats, he’s incredibly transactional, and he can change on a dime. And if he wants to get something done or Hakeem Jeffries says something nice about him, he would be totally willing to forget Hakeem standing in front of a microphone and saying, “F Donald Trump,” right? Now I’ll move on to dystopia. Rosin: Okay. Bring it. Parker: There’s certainly the congressional investigations, and then the potential constitutional crisis, I guess would be the right word, if subpoenas are issued and people from Trump’s administration or former administration officials fail to appear before Congress, and then the recourse that Congress has is to kick it up to a Trump Justice Department, where his key metric on hiring an attorney general is that they will be loyal to him, à la a fixer, not an independent attorney general. So you have that. So if we get to that point, it will be fascinating to see what happens. There’s also, and again, when I was talking to people about this before, I don’t think anyone was imagining the magnitude of the Democratic wins we saw Tuesday night, but Donald Trump at his core is not like an LBJ-style legislator, right? It’s not that he had broad plans for Obamacare and now he’s never gonna be able to push it through Congress, right? Yes, there are areas where he could make deals, but Donald Trump, even with a Republican Congress where he ostensibly could have gotten more things done, basically was willing to try to go around Congress, flex his muscle, use the levers, use executive authority, push through laws, boundaries, standards, norms. It might be a little harder to do with Democrats, but Congress holds the purse strings to declare war. Does that mean Trump can’t launch another war? No. And so you could just see someone who is desperate for relevancy, desperate not to be a lame duck, kind of coming up with every way, shape, or form an outlandish controversy to keep the focus on him as the circus inherently moves on towards 2028, which I think could be frightening for a lot of people. Rosin: Right, and then the Democrats get drawn into that three and a half minutes of time, rather than their 30 seconds of time. I mean, that’s that scenario where Trump keeps creating crisis and disaster after crisis and disaster. Scherer: He has not been on the national stage yet without monopolizing our attention, and I don’t think there’s a scenario where he suddenly gets quiet. Parker: I think one concern is that the gambits might need to get bolder for him to keep our attention. So is it invading Canada to make it a 51st state that is the thing that, say, takes away attention from J. D. Vance and Marco Rubio duking it out for the party’s nominee? I think that is a doomsday scenario. Rosin: Okay, that’s Trump. Let me just ask you about the Republican Party. It’s unclear who a party leader is now. Like, he has control of a lot of the money. He is the president. Then you can already see J. D. Vance and other people vying for attention. If you’re a Republican, where is the first place you focus your energies? Is it finding a new leader? Is it 2028? What is your next move? Scherer: I think there’s a lot of time for 2028, and mainly because I think the president wants that to be drawn out. He doesn’t wanna have that solved anytime soon. He’s not gonna be endorsing early next year. So that’s a 2027, 2028 question. I think the immediate concern of Republican lawmakers is to figure out how to solve the problem. One of the big takeaways of this election is how quickly parties can heal themselves, how quickly they can pivot and change. I mean, the Democratic Party that just won is so far from Joe Biden’s Democratic Party, and we’re coming out of, you know, 18 months of everyone saying on every podcast and every article that no one likes Democrats. Everybody hates Democrats, you know? The Democrats polling has never been lower . Parker: Which is still true. ( Laughs .) Scherer: Which is still true. But parties know how to adapt, and they change, and they transform, and they morph. And so the immediate project of the Republican Party is to figure out how to do that over the next six months to a year, and how to do that while navigating the president. The biggest affordability piece of legislation this year was a housing bill—bipartisan bill, huge majorities in the House and Senate of Republicans and Democrats, sponsored by far-left liberal Elizabeth Warren—that got passed, and President Trump would not sign it. And the reason he wouldn’t sign it was he was upset with Senate Republicans that they wouldn’t pass his election-reform bill. He was just in a different universe, totally disconnected from the needs of voters. And I think that’s the issue that Republicans are gonna be fighting over over the next six months. They have to figure out how to actually be able to do stuff and be on the right message and not have it all be about the next steel beam in the ballroom. Parker: But I would still stipulate—and this is gonna be a challenge for Republicans—that Donald Trump is still the leader of the Republican Party. They may not like it, he may not be as powerful, and he may not lead that full coalition that helped elect him and Republicans in 2024, but Donald Trump is the leader of the Republican Party. You even look at the names who are getting floated for the next—I guess it’s no longer House speaker, but, you know—House minority leader, and it’s Jim Jordan, who is a Trump-lite ally. So he is still the leader, and they’re going to have to grapple with how much they wanna be led by him, how much they wanna distance themselves, if and how and where they can push back. Rosin: All right, that’s the Republicans. Let’s now end by talking about the Democrats. The message they have for sure is voters don’t like the status quo. They do not have a message yet that voters love Democrats. Because one thing that I’ve thought about this election: It was such a big swing that it was almost destabilizing. Like, there’s no ground under your feet. It felt like the political equivalent of a rebound relationship— Parker: ( Laughs .) Rosin: —which everybody understands. It’s a bad idea. It never goes well, and it doesn’t last. Parker: It’s heady and it’s intoxicating and it’s about to blow up. Rosin: Exactly. So let’s talk about that. What exactly do voters expect from Democrats, and what’s the delicate balance they have to do? Parker: What they expect, that’s very easy: They expect lower prices. Rosin: Concretely. Like, I literally have to go into the grocery store and go to the gas station and see that my prices are lower? Because that’s much smaller than the vast inequality between you and tech titans that was the message that Hakeem Jeffries was pushing. Parker: Sure, and Michael may disagree with me, but I think first off, the immediate pocketbook—when people cannot afford to buy a house, or move out of their house, or fill up their car, or provide groceries for their family when they’re working two or three jobs, that trumps whether or not Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos are getting even further away from us mere mortals. I mean, that’s an existential concern compared to a tangible concern. And I think the way Democrats get in trouble is because this wave was so sweeping. In certain ways, they can learn the lessons, as we reported, of Hakeem Jeffries and staying unified on costs and things like that. But there is sort of enough in there for everyone to claim, for the democratic socialists to claim that it’s not just populism, but it really is liberalism and progressivism, and that trans issues are an equally valid place for them to fight over. And I think that is gonna be a problem for Democrats. Plus—and this is always true, and this was true in talking to people for this story—it is always harder to govern and message when you’re governing than to just sort of point out what’s wrong with things. Scherer: One of the first things Jeffries said after Trump was inaugurated was, Look at what’s happened over the last 40 years. We go from Clinton to Bush to Obama to Trump to Biden to Trump . Voters are saying the same thing at almost every election. A couple of them had two terms, but almost every election. Rosin: Change. Scherer: Yeah, change. We don’t like the way things are going. In almost every one of those elections, economic concerns, rising prices, health-care costs, all that stuff, that’s the issue. And so the trap, the danger Democrats are facing is it’s not clear there is a fix to this. I mean, it’s not clear that politicians have the power to solve the illness that the American people are suffering. Now, what they can do is they can fight against the Iran war on the premise that if they fight against the Iran war, they’re gonna be lowering gas prices. That’s one you can see very quickly. Everyone cares about it because it’s actually on the street when they drive by. They’ve talked about trying to reinstitute some of the Medicaid cuts that were cut, and go after the Obamacare subsidies. There’s gonna be talk about new entitlements and things like that. I mean, that’s the project they have. And in the same way that the campaign made lots of issues into affordability issues, corruption, all this other stuff, I think Democrats will be making lots of legislative policy arguments and claiming these are affordability issues. And the question is whether voters still feel like they’re fighting harder for this in a year, and give them a mandate to have a president and two houses of Congress, which would actually give them the ability to do something big again. Rosin: Yeah, that’s essentially the pitfall that I see. It’s the danger of populism. What you guys described as the successful message is the fundamentally populist message. It’s not just that you’re suffering; it’s that there’s an enemy, and that’s always a very convincing story. The Democrats swap the enemy from, you know, immigrants who are stealing your jobs to tech giants who are stealing your jobs. That is the message that resonates now. But it’s not necessarily completely true. The reasons for inequality are deep and structural, and they really do go beyond data centers. And so that’s why it seems to me voters want something huge from Democrats that is actually a very long-term American project that’s not gonna happen in two years or four years. Parker: Yeah, and the solutions are often wonky and complicated and incremental. Scherer: And the other thing is that we may be on the verge of a real economic change coming in the next two years before the next election, with AI, that resets the whole table for us. I mean, we could have really large layoffs in a year or two. I mean, the amount of economic pain we’re in right now could be much worse in two years. I don’t—I can’t predict these things, but I think this is still a very fluid situation. But I totally agree with you. The problem is so much greater than the capacity of the political system to solve it. But it’s also true that if you wanna be successful in this political system, you have to be focused on that problem. [ Music ] Rosin: Well, Ashley, thank you for joining me. Parker: Thank you for having me. Rosin: Michael, thank you. Scherer: Thank you. Rosin: This episode of Radio Atlantic was produced by Jinae West and Rosie Hughes. It was edited by Kevin Townsend. Fact-checking by Sam Fentress. Rob Smierciak engineered and provided original music. We also had music from Breakmaster Cylinder. Claudine Ebeid is the executive producer of Atlantic audio, and Andrea Valdez is our managing editor. Listeners, if you enjoy the show, you can support our work and the work of all Atlantic journalists when you subscribe to The Atlantic at TheAtlantic.com/Listener . I’m Hanna Rosin. Thank you for listening.

items.title: Pakistan, UK agree to deepen cooperation in security, trade and migration
items.description: Pakistan and the United Kingdom on Thursday agreed to deepen cooperation in multiple areas, according to the Foreign Office (FO). According to the FO, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar received the visiting UK minister of state for security, Dan Jarvis, in Islamabad, where both sides reviewed existing bilateral ties and agreed to “further deepen cooperation in security, law enforcement, migration, trade and investment”. Dar and Jarvis also exchanged views on regional and global developments and discussed further meetings under the R4 + E4 framework, the statement added, referring to a meeting of the two regional groups in Istanbul last month. “Dar underscored the importance of continued Pakistan-UK cooperation on bilateral matters and on regional developments of mutual interest,” the FO said. A day prior, Pakistan and the UK expressed concern at terrorism emanating from Afghanistan during their annual bilateral counter-terrorism dialogue in Islamabad, the FO stated. “The two sides discussed in detail the evolving regional and global security environment and exchanged views on the threats posed by terrorist entities, including transnational terrorist networks,” it said. “Both sides expressed concerns over the continuing threat posed by terrorist groups, including the Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan, operating in and from Afghanistan,” the FO said, adding that they underscored the “urgent need for a stable, secure Afghanistan as a cornerstone for lasting peace and prosperity across the region”. Islamabad and London have also been engaged in the Enhanced Strategic Dialogue since 2011, which has deepened and broadened the dialogue between the two countries, covering areas such as trade, economic growth and development, cultural cooperation, security, and education.

items.title: Burundi : l’autonomisation, la famille et le développement au centre du septième forum de haut niveau des femmes leaders
items.description: Pour sa septieme edition, le forum de haut niveau des femmes leaders, organise du 4 au 5 novembre au Burundi, sous l'egide de l'Office de la Premiere dame pour le developpement (OPDD) et sous le haut patronage du president de la Republique du Burundi et president en exercice de l'Union africaine (UA), evariste Ndayishimiye, a pris pour theme : « Autonomisation des jeunes filles et des femmes : levier strategique pour le developpement du capital humain et le renforcement de la resilience face aux changements climatiques ». De hautes personnalites feminines africaines assistent au forum. Le 3 novembre, la Premiere dame du Burundi Angeline Ndayishimiye a accueilli a l'aeroport international Melchior Ndadaye de Bujumbura son homologue de la Republique centrafricaine, Brigitte Touadera, celle d'Angola Ana Dias Lourenco, ainsi que celle du Senegal Marie Khone Faye. Retour en images sur l’accueil chaleureux réservé aux Premières Dames d’Afrique, ce 03.11.2026, venues au Burundi pour prendre part aux activités de la 7ᵉ édition du Forum de Haut Niveau des Femmes Leaders. https://t.co/c8eFxJKfnF — OPDD-Burundi (@OPDD_Burundi) November 3, 2026 « Qui rate une bonne femme, rate la richesse » Dans son discours prononce lors du forum, Angeline Ndayishimiye a appele les femmes a elaborer des projets de developpement et a s'impliquer dans la protection de l'environnement. Citant le vieil adage local « Qui rate une bonne femme, rate la richesse », la Premiere dame a rappele l'apport irremplacable des femmes a l'essor des foyers, des familles, du pays, de l'Afrique et du monde. Les grands moments de la première journée du Forum de Haut Niveau des Femmes Leaders 2026. https://t.co/EWvzjD1PrV — OPDD-Burundi (@OPDD_Burundi) November 4, 2026 Revenant sur le theme de l'evenement, elle a declare : « Nous nous sommes rassembles dans ce forum pour soutenir la femme, afin qu'elle puisse s'autonomiser, faire grandir sa famille et developper son pays », precisant que l'objet du forum n'est pas le fruit du hasard dans la mesure ou il permet de soulever les nombreux defis auxquels sont confrontees les femmes qui transmettent l'education a leurs enfants, comme premiere richesse, tout en creant une autre richesse pour l'avenir en lancant des entreprises ou des usines. La Premiere dame burundaise a souligne qu'une femme qui produit et entreprend assure la stabilite de la famille et renforce le pays. L'autonomisation economique des femmes : « une condition de paix durable » Pour le president de la commission de la Communaute economique des etats de l'Afrique centrale (CEEAC) Ezechiel Nibigira, « aucune nation ne peut pretendre a un developpement durable sans mobiliser pleinement le potentiel de ses filles et de ses femmes ». Il a affirme que dans ce contexte, que les femmes ne sont pas que des victimes du changement climatique, mais qu'elles sont surtout les actrices des solutions durables, soulignant que « l'autonomisation economique des femmes n'est pas une faveur. C'est un imperatif economique et une condition de paix durable ». Face aux sécheresses et aux inondations les femmes doivent devenir des actrices majeures de la résilience climatique. Son Excellence Angeline Ndayishimiye les a encouragé à s'engager dans la protection de l'environnement et l'adoption de pratiques agricoles durables. #FFL7 https://t.co/RujH5akvxq — OPDD-Burundi (@OPDD_Burundi) November 4, 2026 Pour sa part, la coordonnatrice residente du systeme des Nations unies au Burundi Violet Kakyomya a salue l'engagement de la Premiere dame en faveur de la sante, de l'education et de l'autonomisation des femmes. « Si je suis aujourd'hui devant vous, c'est parce que j'ai eu acces a l'education. L'education m'a donne des connaissances, mais aussi une voix », a-t-elle indique, ajoutant que l'autonomisation des femmes se fonde sur l'education, avant de deboucher sur de veritables opportunites d'ordre economique pour toutes les femmes, y compris celles en situation de handicap ou encore les adolescentes meres. Ouverture de la 7ᵉ édition du Forum de Haut Niveau des Femmes Leaders sous le Haut Patronage de Son Excellence Évariste Ndayishimiye, Président de la République du Burundi. https://t.co/f9j7sKyAmD — WHO Burundi (@WhoBurundi) November 5, 2026 En echo, la Dr Liliane Nkengurutse, secretaire executive de l'OPDD-Burundi, avait declare dans une conference de presse la veille du forum que les travaux porteraient notamment sur les politiques et strategies susceptibles de renforcer l'autonomisation economique et sociale des femmes et des jeunes filles, de reduire les inegalites, de lutter contre les violences basees sur le genre et de consolider leur capacite d'adaptation aux effets des changements climatiques. Les problematiques seront d'ailleurs abordees en profondeur en marge du forum lors d'une rencontre dediee au theme « L'autonomisation des jeunes filles, levier strategique pour le developpement du capital humain et le renforcement de la resilience face au changement climatique ». Une campagne intitulee « Building Resilience » Organisation des Premieres dames d'Afrique pour le developpement (OPDAD) et du salon international de l'entrepreneuriat feminin de la CEEAC est aussi prevue dans le cadre de l'evenement.

items.title: Adhésion à l’UE : Bruxelles constate l’échec de Kiev sur la majorité des réformes anticorruption
items.description: L'Ukraine prend du retard sur la Moldavie dans la course a l'Union europeenne , rapporte le Financial Times le 5 novembre. Chisinau pourrait achever les negociations debut 2028. Kiev vise la fin de la meme annee, mais Bruxelles reclame un rythme plus soutenu. En 2027, la Moldavie pourrait clore 25 chapitres de negociation, contre sept pour l'Ukraine. Dix reformes encore en attente Le rapport europeen du 4 novembre dresse une liste precise des retards. La plupart des dix reformes prioritaires convenues avec les autorites ukrainiennes en decembre 2025 restent a accomplir. La Commission europeenne ecrit : « Aucune loi n'a ete adoptee pour faire progresser le cadre juridique de la lutte contre la corruption. L'Ukraine devrait intensifier ses efforts dans ce domaine, a titre prioritaire. » La nouvelle strategie nationale pour 2026-2030 attend toujours un vote du Parlement. Autre constat de Bruxelles : en 2025, dix prevenus poursuivis dans des dossiers de corruption de haut niveau ont echappe a la responsabilite penale en raison de la prescription. La Commission demande de revoir les delais de procedure et les regles qui entraînent la cloture automatique de certaines affaires. Le meme rapport indique : « Les institutions de lutte contre la corruption ont poursuivi leurs rapports faisant etat de pressions exercees par des institutions publiques, des forces de l'ordre et des agences de securite. Elles se trouvent globalement dans une situation delicate. » Bruxelles evoque aussi la surveillance d'agents du Bureau national anticorruption (NABU) et demande d'etendre ses competences a l'administration presidentielle. Midas, jusqu'au sommet du pouvoir Le rapport cite l'operation Midas , une enquete sur des faits de corruption et de blanchiment dans les marches publics de l'energie et de la defense. Le scandale a entraîne les departs de ministres, du chef de l'administration presidentielle et d'autres hauts responsables. Bruxelles mentionne egalement des enquetes visant des deputes, des magistrats et des procureurs. Le 4 novembre, le NABU et le Parquet specialise anticorruption ont annonce la cloture de leur enquete sur Midas. Selon les enqueteurs, des fournisseurs de l'entreprise ukrainienne Energoatom etaient contraints de payer des commissions de 10 a 15 %. Le NABU fait etat de plus de 111 millions de dollars et 12 millions d'euros ayant circule dans le reseau. Parmi les personnes mises en cause figure Timour Minditch, ancien associe de Volodymyr Zelensky. En Ukraine, la corruption reste problematique dans l'energie, la defense et la construction, constate Bruxelles.

items.title: Cristiano Ronaldo raccroche définitivement les crampons avec le Portugal
items.description: C’est une page monumentale du football portugais qui se tourne. À 41 ans, Cristiano Ronaldo a annoncé, ce jeudi 5 novembre 2026, sa retraite internationale. Une décision dévoilée sur son compte Instagram, selon plusieurs médias, qui met fin à plus de deux décennies d’une aventure exceptionnelle avec la Seleção. Le quintuple Ballon d’Or quitte ainsi la scène internationale avec un palmarès historique, 234 sélections et 146 buts au compteur. Le clap de fin pour Cristiano Ronaldo sous le maillot du Portugal. Après plus de vingt ans de bons et loyaux services, la superstar portugaise a décidé de mettre un terme à sa carrière internationale. «Aujourd'hui, mon voyage avec la sélection nationale arrive à sa fin», a déclaré l'attaquant dans une vidéo publiée sur ses réseaux sociaux. Dans un message adressé «aux Portugais» sur Instagram, le capitaine emblématique de la Seleção a fait savoir que cette décision n'avait pas été facile à prendre. «Cela n'a pas été une décision facile», a-t-il confié, estimant que le moment était désormais venu de transmettre, «pour l'avenir», le maillot national qu'il a porté pendant plus de deux décennies. Cette annonce intervient dans un contexte particulièrement tendu entre le joueur et sa sélection. Elle survient plusieurs semaines après un épisode de tensions qui avait fait grand bruit, marqué notamment par son départ du rassemblement national à la suite d'un différend avec son sélectionneur, lors de la dernière fenêtre internationale de la Ligue des nations. Une légende aux chiffres vertigineux Avec 234 rencontres disputées et 146 buts inscrits sous les couleurs portugaises, Cristiano Ronaldo s'en va en laissant une empreinte indélébile dans l'histoire de sa sélection. Meilleur buteur de tous les temps du Portugal, l'ancien attaquant du Real Madrid aura été l'un des grands artisans des plus belles pages du football lusitanien. Son parcours international restera notamment marqué par le sacre historique à l'Euro 2016, premier titre continental du Portugal, ainsi que par la victoire en Ligue des nations en 2019. À 41 ans, celui qui aura longtemps incarné les ambitions et les espoirs de tout un peuple choisit donc de passer le témoin. Si son histoire avec la Seleção s'achève, son héritage, lui, est appelé à traverser les générations. Cristiano Ronaldo quitte la scène internationale, mais son nom restera gravé parmi les plus grandes légendes du football. items.title: Électricité | La Tunisie va se doter d’une capacité de stockage de 150 MW avant l’été 2027
items.description: La Tunisie accélère le développement du stockage de l’énergie électrique afin de renforcer la sécurité des approvisionnements, de prévenir les coupures de courant et de favoriser l’intégration des sources d’énergie renouvelables au réseau national. La Société tunisienne de l’électricité et du gaz (Steg) a lancé un appel d’offres international pour la réalisation de dix systèmes de stockage par batteries, dotés d’une puissance totale de 300 mégawatts (MW) et d’une capacité de stockage de 600 mégawattheures (MWh). Le projet, désigné sous le nom de «Battery Energy Storage Systems» (Bess), prévoit la réalisation des installations «clés en main» , couvrant la conception, la fourniture des équipements, l’installation, la mise en service et la maintenance. Cet investissement vise à accroître la flexibilité du système électrique tunisien, en permettant de stocker l’énergie disponible durant les périodes de faible consommation ou de forte production, pour la réinjecter sur le réseau lors des pics de demande. Selon l’appel d’offres de la Steg, référencé sous le numéro 2026 E 4017, les interventions seront réparties en trois lots géographiques. Dans le Nord, quatre installations sont prévues à Ben Arous, Gaâfour, Mateur et Kchabta, totalisant 105 MW et 210 MWh. Dans le Centre, les sites concernés sont Msaken, Ksour Essef et Bir Lahfey, avec 90 MW et 180 MWh. Enfin, dans le Sud, des installations seront réalisées à Gabès Sud, Médenine et Midoun-Djerba, pour une capacité supplémentaire de 105 MW et 210 MWh. Chaque système sera dimensionné pour délivrer sa puissance nominale pendant environ deux heures, contribuant ainsi à la stabilité de la fréquence et de la tension du réseau, ainsi qu’à la gestion des écarts entre la production et la consommation. Les batteries pourront également absorber une partie de l’électricité produite par les installations photovoltaïques durant les heures de fort ensoleillement, pour la rendre disponible en soirée. L’appel d’offres, publié en septembre, prévoit désormais la soumission des offres au plus tard le 11 novembre à 9h30, suite à une prolongation de l’échéance initiale, fixée au 29 octobre. L’ouverture des offres technico-financières est prévue le même jour, à 10h00, au siège de la Steg à Tunis. Les candidatures devront être transmises via la plateforme nationale des marchés publics, Tuneps. Électricité | Tourner la page des coupures et planifier l’été 2027 Le ministre par intérim de l’Industrie, des Mines et de l’Énergie, Salah Zouari, s’exprimant le 3 novembre devant les commissions parlementaires compétentes, a fait état de l’objectif d’installer une première tranche de batteries d’une capacité de 150 MW avant l’été 2027 — avec une mise en service progressive — afin d’atteindre, par la suite, une puissance totale d’au moins 300 MW. Cette initiative s’inscrit dans le programme gouvernemental visant à répondre aux besoins croissants en électricité et à réduire le risque de nouvelles coupures programmées, suite aux difficultés rencontrées durant l’été 2026. La Tunisie continue, en effet, de recourir aux importations d’électricité en provenance d’Algérie pour compenser le déséquilibre entre la production nationale et la demande. Le gouvernement tunisien a placé le développement des capacités de stockage parmi les priorités de sa stratégie énergétique, laquelle prévoit également le renforcement des centrales existantes et une augmentation de la production issue de sources renouvelables, avec pour objectif d’atteindre 35 % d’électricité verte d’ici 2030. Les batteries ne produiront pas d’énergie nouvelle, mais permettront une utilisation plus efficace de l’énergie déjà disponible, faisant du stockage un levier stratégique pour assurer la continuité du service électrique et favoriser la transition énergétique du pays. I. B. L’article Électricité | La Tunisie va se doter d’une capacité de stockage de 150 MW avant l’été 2027 est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Après des années d’interruption, le lycée-collège de Boukaria reconnecté au monde numérique
items.description: Ce mardi 3 novembre 2026 restera gravé dans les annales de l’histoire de Bouré Boukaria, dans la préfecture de Kintinian. Dans l’enceinte de cet établissement d’enseignement général, les portes du centre informatique se sont rouvertes, marquant le début d’une nouvelle ère. Longtemps plongé dans l’obscurité et l’inactivité, faute d’électricité, ce joyau technologique renaît de ses cendres grâce à l’intervention salutaire de l’ONG française Enfant de l’Air (EDA). Une résurrection qui illustre la force de la coopération internationale au service de l’éducation en milieu rural. Bien construit et équipé vers 2017 par la SAG, le centre informatique de Boukaria n’avait connu qu’une brève période d’activité avant de sombrer dans le silence, victime de coupures d’électricité. Face à ce gâchis technologique, l’ONG EDA est venue au secours de l’établissement pour orchestrer un véritable sauvetage technique et pédagogique. Ce renouveau repose sur une alliance financière et écologique exemplaire. EDA a pris en charge 90 % du financement, complétés par l’effort des parents d’élèves, à travers une contribution de 10 % du bureau de l’APEAE. Pour conjurer définitivement le spectre des pannes de courant, le centre a été doté d’une autonomie énergétique totale grâce à l’installation de panneaux solaires de dernière génération et de batteries au lithium performantes. Au-delà du matériel, le système informatique a été entièrement actualisé grâce à l’intégration de nouveaux logiciels d’apprentissage, rigoureusement alignés sur les programmes d’enseignement officiels en vigueur. Sous le slogan évocateur « La pédagogie avec le numérique », l’ONG EDA ne s’est pas contentée d’installer les machines. Durant deux semaines intensives, les formateurs français ont partagé bénévolement leur expertise, à leurs propres frais. Au cœur de cette transmission, un enseignant en activité au sein de l’établissement, M. Abdourahamane Camara, a bénéficié d’un accompagnement particulier de la part de ces experts. Il a reçu le flambeau de la connaissance afin d’assurer, avec rigueur, la transmission des acquis à ses pairs après le départ de l’ONG. La cérémonie de réinauguration a mobilisé toutes les forces vives de la localité, sous l’égide de la Direction préfectorale de l’éducation (DPE) de Siguiri, représentée par le chef de la section pédagogique, M. Amara Tenguiano. À ses côtés figuraient le représentant de M. le préfet par intérim de Kintinian, le représentant de M. le maire, chaleureusement salué pour son écoute et son dévouement envers la localité, les présidents de districts ainsi que Mme Kankou Kourouma, représentante du département APC de la SAG. Tous ont rehaussé l’événement de leur présence. Prenant la parole, le proviseur du lycée-collège, M. Aboubacar Diakité, dont la clairvoyance a été le moteur de cette réussite, a prononcé un discours court, mais mémorable. En seulement quatre minutes d’une allocution engagée et responsable, il a exhorté la communauté scolaire à prendre soin de ces bijoux technologiques et à s’investir pleinement dans la formation continue. La transition vers la pratique s’est ensuite opérée à travers des simulations d’enseignement numérique en classe, fascinant les invités et redonnant le sourire aux élèves, désormais connectés au monde. L’inauguration du centre informatique de Bouré Boukaria n’est pas un aboutissement, mais le prélude à une ambition plus vaste, l’ONG EDA projetant déjà d’étendre cette initiative à d’autres localités de la zone de Bouré. Cette belle réussite locale résonne harmonieusement avec la vision nationale portée au sommet de l’État par Son Excellence Madame la ministre Bintou Kéïta, en charge de l’Éducation nationale, de l’Alphabétisation, de l’Enseignement technique et de la Formation professionnelle. À travers le pays, les réformes courageuses engagées par la ministre s’emploient à briser les barrières de l’isolement géographique. En apportant la lumière du numérique au cœur des zones rurales, des initiatives comme celle de Boukaria prouvent que l’école guinéenne avance résolument vers la modernité, l’équité et l’excellence. Mamoudou Kéïta, correspondant basé dans la préfecture de Kintinian 628 61 88 90 L’article Après des années d’interruption, le lycée-collège de Boukaria reconnecté au monde numérique est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .
